cards.front: Recall a key point about Ethical and Environmental Considerations
cards.back: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) means businesses consider their impact on society and the environment, not just profit.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Ethical and Environmental Considerations
cards.back: Ethical issues include: fair pay and working conditions, avoiding sweatshops, honest advertising, paying fair taxes, and sourcing materials responsibly.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Ethical and Environmental Considerations
cards.back: Environmental considerations include: reducing carbon footprint, recycling, sustainable sourcing, minimising waste, and complying with environmental laws.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Ethical and Environmental Considerations
cards.back: Pressure groups can influence business behaviour through campaigns, boycotts, and negative publicity - e.g. Greenpeace targeting companies with poor environmental records.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Ethical and Environmental Considerations
cards.back: Fair trade ensures producers in developing countries receive a fair price, improving living standards and community investment.

cards.front: What should you know about business exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating ethical decisions, use the SPIR framework: Stakeholders (who is affected?), Profit (financial impact?), Image (reputation effect?), Responsibility (legal/moral obligations?). Conclude by weighing short-term costs against long-term benefits.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Ethical businesses always make less profit because ethical choices cost more. Correct: Ethical choices can increase costs short-term but may boost revenue long-term through: brand loyalty from conscious consumers, reduced staff turnover, avoiding fines/scandals, and attracting investors who value ESG criteria.
